kernels.definition: Earth is layered into a thin outer crust, a thick rocky mantle, and a metallic core; the upper mantle's asthenosphere is solid rock that flows slowly by convection.

definitionAnchor.quote: The outermost chemical layer and the one we currently reside on is the crust

facts.text: The mantle sits below the crust and above the core.

anchor.quote: The mantle sits below the crust and above the core

facts.text: The core has both liquid and solid layers and is made mostly of iron and nickel.

anchor.quote: The core of the Earth has both liquid and solid layers and consists mostly of iron, nickel, and possibly some oxygen

facts.text: The asthenosphere is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat.

anchor.quote: this layer moves and flows due to convection currents created by heat coming from the earth's core

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.1 Earth's interior

kernels.definition: Plate tectonics holds that Earth's rigid lithosphere is broken into plates that move over the ductile asthenosphere; most geologic action occurs at their three kinds of boundaries.

definitionAnchor.quote: Plate boundaries are where most of Earth's geologic action occurs

facts.text: At divergent boundaries, lithospheric plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created.

anchor.quote: At divergent boundaries, sometimes called constructive boundaries, lithospheric plates move away from each other

facts.text: At convergent boundaries, two or more plates move toward each other and lithosphere is destroyed.

anchor.quote: Convergent boundaries, also called destructive boundaries, are places where two or more plates move toward each other

facts.text: At a transform boundary, plates slide horizontally past each other.

anchor.quote: A transform boundary is where the lithospheric plates slide past each other in the horizontal plane

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.4 Plate boundaries

kernels.definition: An earthquake releases stored elastic energy when rock slips along a fault; the energy travels outward as seismic waves, including fast compressional P waves and slower shear S waves.

definitionAnchor.quote: Earthquakes are felt at the surface of the Earth when energy is released by blocks of rock sliding past each other, i.e. faulting has occurred

facts.text: Elastic rebound theory explains earthquakes: stored energy is released and the broken rock springs back toward its original position.

anchor.quote: The release of seismic energy is explained by the elastic rebound theory

facts.text: P waves are the fastest body waves and move by compression, like sound through air, so they travel through solids, liquids, and gases.

anchor.quote: enabling them to travel through solids, liquids, plasma, and gases

facts.text: S waves are slower shear waves restricted to lateral motion, so they travel only through solids, never liquids.

anchor.quote: S waves can only travel through solids but not liquids, plasma, or gases

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §9.1 Earthquakes and seismic waves

mcItems.q: A lab group notes a rock layer that lies below the crust and above the core. Which Earth layer is this?
mcItems.ex: The mantle fits because it is the layer below the crust and above the core. A common misconception is to choose the core because it is deeper, but the core is below the mantle, not between crust and core.

mcItems.q: A student describes a region of the upper mantle as solid rock that flows slowly because of convection. Which layer is being described?
mcItems.ex: The asthenosphere is correct because it is mechanically weak solid rock that moves slowly by convection currents driven by heat from the core. A plausible misconception is the lithosphere, but that layer is not the one identified here as the flowing upper mantle region.

keyTerms.df: A mechanically weak upper-mantle zone that behaves like solid rock while moving slowly.
keyTerms.eg: Hot mantle material beneath a plate can circulate through the asthenosphere.
keyTerms.mi: It is liquid magma.
keyTerms.cx: It is solid rock that flows slowly by convection, not a liquid layer.

keyTerms.df: The planet’s central metallic region, made mostly of iron and nickel and divided into liquid and solid layers.
keyTerms.eg: Seismic evidence shows distinct liquid and solid parts within the deep center of Earth.
keyTerms.mi: It is a single uniform solid sphere.
keyTerms.cx: It has both liquid and solid layers, and it is mostly iron and nickel.

mcItems.q: A field map shows two oceanic plates separating and a broad band of fresh rock forming between them. Which boundary best matches this pattern?
mcItems.ex: Divergent boundaries fit because plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created. A common misconception is to call any plate edge convergent, but convergence involves plates moving toward each other and destroying lithosphere instead.

mcItems.q: Two crustal blocks are offset along a fault, and repeated measurements show they move side by side with little change in distance between them. What boundary is indicated?
mcItems.ex: Transform boundaries match lateral slipping, where plates slide horizontally past each other. The likely misconception is to confuse sideways motion with spreading or collision; those belong to divergent and convergent boundaries, respectively.

keyTerms.df: The rigid outer layer broken into moving plates.
keyTerms.eg: A tectonic plate in a lab map represents part of the lithosphere.
keyTerms.mi: It is a single continuous shell with no breaks.
keyTerms.cx: It is divided into plates that shift over the ductile asthenosphere.

keyTerms.df: A plate boundary where adjacent plates move sideways past one another.
keyTerms.eg: A fault zone where two blocks slide horizontally with little opening or closing.
keyTerms.mi: It means plates are colliding or pulling apart.
keyTerms.cx: Sideways motion defines transform motion; collision and separation describe convergent and divergent boundaries.

mcItems.q: A field station records seismic arrivals from a distant earthquake. Which interpretation best fits the first body wave to arrive at the station?
op: It is a P wave, because compressional waves travel fastest through solids, liquids, and gases.
It is an S wave, because shear waves arrive first after moving through any material.
It is a surface wave, because surface waves always outrun body waves.
It is a P wave, because compressional waves travel only through solids.
mcItems.ex: The first arrival is best explained as a P wave: it is the fastest body wave and can travel through solids, liquids, and gases. A common misconception is that all seismic waves behave like S waves, but S waves are slower and cannot move through liquids.

mcItems.q: After a fault slips during an earthquake, what best explains the release of stored elastic energy?
op: The broken rock springs back toward its original position as stress is released.
The rock melts, so energy escapes as lava flow.
The fault locks more tightly, storing additional elastic energy.
The energy stops at the fault and does not travel outward.
mcItems.ex: Elastic rebound theory says earthquakes happen when stored energy is released and the broken rock springs back toward its original position. A likely misconception is that the fault simply remains in place after slipping; instead, the released energy travels outward as seismic waves.

keyTerms.df: A faulted rock mass releases stored strain and then springs back toward its earlier shape.
keyTerms.eg: In a lab model, a bent block suddenly slips and then recoils after the stress drops.
keyTerms.mi: The idea that earthquakes only happen when rock is permanently crushed.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that elastic strain can be stored and then released when rock slips along a fault.

keyTerms.df: A slower body wave that moves by shear motion.
keyTerms.eg: A seismic record shows this phase arriving after the first compressional pulse at a station in bedrock.
keyTerms.mi: The belief that these waves can pass through liquid layers.
keyTerms.cx: They travel only through solids, never through liquids.
